lesson.menu_title: The Panel — Four People, One Answer
lesson.menu_desc: Answering the person who asked and the room at the same time, and repeating an answer word for word -- 30 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 14 -- The Panel
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Fernando Meneghelli Bottura | Lesson 14 -- The Panel

listenings.text: In a panel I am usually the one who says the least, and I decide more than people expect. What I write down is not the answer. It is who the candidate is talking to. The ones who do this badly answer only the person who asked, and the rest of us stop listening within a minute. The ones who do it well look at the person who asked, give the first line to them, and then give the rest to the room. The other thing I write down is what happens when two of us ask about the same thing. If the candidate gives a different answer the second time, that is a bigger problem for me than a weak answer given twice. Consistency is the only thing four people can compare afterwards.

Panels overlap, and we know it. Two of us will ask about the same decision from different angles, and a third will ask it again at the end because he was writing when you answered. The candidates who survive that do one small thing: they say out loud that the question has come up before, without any irritation, and they give the same answer in the same words. Something like, that is the same decision we were discussing earlier, and the number is still sixty days. It sounds obvious. Almost nobody does it. What most people do is add something new the second time, to make it more interesting, and that is when four people start comparing notes and finding two versions.

extra_audio.text: The chair opens and asks about the first ninety days. Fernando answers her first, and then gives the rest to the room. The chair starts to bring the operations director in. Fernando asks to finish the cash part, in one sentence. He comes back out loud to the part of the question he had not answered.
